subtopic: FEED GRAIN
speechtext: On what foods is the federal eight per cent sales tax now levied?

subtopic: FEED GRAIN
speechtext:
The structure of the act is such that all goods manufactured or imported are subject to sales tax unless they are included in the list of articles specifically exempted therefrom. It is therefore not possible to give a comprehensive list of articles to which the tax applies.
The question, however, might best be answered by enumerating the foods which are exempted from the tax, as follows:
Barley; bread; butter; cheese; cream; eggs, egg albumen and egg yolks; glucose; honey; ice; lactose; lard; rice; salt; soups; split peas; sugar; yeast; yogurt.
Baker's cakes and pies, including biscuits, cookies or other similar articles.
Cereal breakfast foods, not including beverages.
Fish and other edible products thereof.
Flour, including pastry, cake, biscuit, and similar mixes.
Foods prepared and sold exclusively for feeding infants.
Fruit, fresh, canned, frozen, dried or evaporated.
Grain grits and meals.
Jams, jellies, marmalades, and preserves.
Malt syrup, except when sold for beverage purposes.
Maple syrup; corn syrup; table syrups; molasses, and materials to be used exclusively in the manufacture thereof.
Meats and poultry, fresh, cooked, canned, frozen, smoked or dried.
Milk, including buttermilk, condensed milk, evaporated milk, and powdered milk.
Peanut butter and shortening and materials for use exclusively in the manufacture thereof.
Spaghetti, macaroni, and vermicelli.
Vegetables, fresh, canned, frozen or dehydrated, not including pickles, relishes, catsup, sauces, olives, horse-radish, mustard, and similar goods.
Vegetable juices; fruit juices which consist of at least ninety-five per cent of pure juice of the fruit.

maintopic: CO-OPERATION WITH MANITOBA HEALTH AUTHORITIES IN PREVENTION OF DISEASE
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In view of the vast bodies of water which have covered fields and flooded houses in Manitoba, and the probability that it will be several weeks after the water level has become stationary before the water is drained away, can the minister make a statement with respect to disease possibilities, and whether the government is in full co-operation with the Manitoba health department with a view to guarding the health of the people of Manitoba?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: CO-OPERATION WITH MANITOBA HEALTH AUTHORITIES IN PREVENTION OF DISEASE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman gave me notice early this morning of this question. I may say, first of all, as I said the other day, that the department of health of the federal government has been in touch with the provincial department of health and has expressed its willingness to do anything within its power to assist that department and that government in meeting the situation which confronts the province of Manitoba at the present time.
Dr. Jackson, who was the former deputy minister ef health for the government of Manitoba, and who is an official of the Department of National Health and Welfare, has just returned from Winnipeg, where he was in consultation with the authorities there. From him I have this report. He points out that the principal health danger is from the contamination of water and food
Inquiries of the Ministry and the spreading of certain diseases, mainly typhoid. He [DOT] states that the two ways to guard against this are, first, to vaccinate people against typhoid, and second, to provide purified water for human consumption.
I may say to my hon. friend that we have been in touch with the principal suppliers of typhoid vaccine in Canada and have been assured that there is no risk of shortage.
Dr. Jackson further reports that through the experience gained in the modified flood in 1948 in the same parts of the province, but not affecting the city of Winnipeg to the same extent, it was possible this time for the provincial department of health immediately to step into the picture as soon as flood waters appeared at Emerson. Every provision was made for a reasonable standard of water for human consumption. Through the co-operation of army officials, chlorinating plants were provided in order that no community would be without properly protected water. The whole sanitary force of the central office of the department, including a sanitary engineer, two district sanitary officers and five sanitary inspectors, were given the responsibility of supervising the control of water supplies and the inspection of foods in the flood areas, as they developed.
I may add that we are following the matter closely in order to see what further co-operation can be extended in the situation.

speechtext: I desire to direct an inquiry either to the Minister of Agriculture or to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, as the case may be. In view of the serious losses sustained last year by many farmers, especially in southwestern Manitoba, from the infestation of aphids, and in view of the report that destruction from the same source is already evident in several states of the union directly south of last year's infested area in Canada, the question I want to ask is this. Is the combating of this insect invasion the responsibility of the federal government or of the provincial government? If of the former, what preparations are being made to meet what may become a serious situation again this year?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: QUESTIONS AS TO INFESTATION OF APHIDS IN SOUTHERN MANITOBA
speechtext:
The responsibility for fighting insects of that kind is a provincial one, but the federal government has always co-operated in every possible way in giving assistance. One of the ways in which we have done that in the past is to examing into what has taken place in the United States and thus to be able to provide any information that may be obtained there which has not already been obtained here through research, to be applied in this country. We have at times assisted in the flying in, where it was necessary, of some of the chemicals which are

essential and which are not available in sufficient quantity. We have assisted in every way possible in doing that, and of course we shall continue to do so in connection with this infestation. I believe that was done last year quite successfully, to the extent that it could be done when the infestation was new; and with the experience of last year I think the provincial government will be able to carry on even more successfully than a year ago. They may be assured of every necessary co-operation.

speechtext:
This is the section which proposes to exempt from the sales tax goods purchased by certain institutions for their own use. With the general intent of the

Excise Tax Act
section I am sure there will be no disagreement whatsoever; on the contrary, there will be the fullest agreement. The question arises, however, as to the scope of the section; and as it appears in section 6 of the bill it seems to me it goes neither as far as was indicated in the discussion of the resolution preceding the bill, nor as far as the present situation warrants.
When the resolution was under discussion on April 27 the parliamentary assistant indicated, broadly, that there were two classes of institutions which it was intended to help by the amendment. The expression he used at page 1974 of Hansard was, "a group of institutions which are closely allied to hospitals". Then, at a later point he said:
The second class to which this section applies is orphanages.
He went on to indicate that it is unfair that institutions in those two classes, namely hospitals and orphanages, should be obliged to pay sales tax in respect of goods purchased by them for their own use. He concluded his remarks on the subject with these words:
But the group of institutions which are covered in this resolution will be carefully enumerated when the actual bill is brought down, and goods bought by those institutions for use in those institutions will be free from sales tax.
If we examine section 6 we see that the benefits of the section are extended to those institutions which are more fully defined in subsection 2. There we see that the exemption applies to institutions-
-certified by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in accordance with regulations of the governor in council to be
(a)	a bona fide public institution whose principal purpose is to provide permanent or semi-permanent shelter and care for children or aged, infirm or incapacitated persons who reside in the institution, and
(b)	in receipt annually of aid from the government of Canada or a province for the maintenance of persons specified in paragraph (a).
My concern directly is with the limitation set out in paragraph Cb) in respect of institutions which are annually in receipt of aid from the government of Canada or a province. I submit those words unduly limit the scope of an otherwise praiseworthy provision. There are many institutions carrying on the most laudable charitable and philanthropic work, of a kind and in a manner which must commend itself to everyone, but which do not receive any annual grant in aid from the government of Canada or the government of any province. As a matter of fact many of the institutions doing the noblest philanthropic and welfare work in Canada are those which are dependent directly upon free contributions from individuals, and those whose only

assistance from the public treasury is derived from municipal governments, not from federal or provincial governments.
The hon. member for Dulferin-Simcoe raised' this question in committee of ways and means during the course of discussion of the resolution, when, as reported at page 1975 of Hansard, he asked:
Old people's homes that are run by a municipality will be included?
The parliamentary assistant replied:
If they receive grants from the municipality by way of assistance, that qualifies them.
I do not find in section 6 any provision which would warrant the drawing of that conclusion from the section. As I read paragraph (b), the scope of the exemption is confined to those institutions otherwise qualified, which receive annual grants from either the government of Canada or the government of a province.
I am sure many representations have been made to the minister in this connection. I know it is a matter of concern to many of the institutions and organizations engaged in welfare work. They are, of course, pleased to see this step being taken, so far as it goes, but in my submission there does not seem to be any reason, if the door is open to admit the exemption in respect of such institutions as receive federal or provincial aid, which would justify the closing of the door-on institutions engaged in just as laudable-and just as necessary work but whose only public assistance is derived from municipal governments.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: QUESTIONS AS TO INFESTATION OF APHIDS IN SOUTHERN MANITOBA
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member for Eglinton has raised this question. It is true that inadvertently I gave that assurance to the hon. member for Dulferin-Simcoe, but I corrected it later in Hansard. The reason I was guilty of this error arose from my background of knowledge of the fact that in the province from which I come any such assistance a municipality may give to a home of this type is matched by the provincial government. I am informed that this condition obtains in other provinces, but not in all of them.
The reason for this limitation to institutions receiving grants from either the federal or a provincial government lies partly in the fact that we find this the most practical way at the present time to define public institutions. In the resolution stage I pointed out that we saw no reason why we should try to help certain of the private hospitals or private old people's homes which are not operated on a charitable basis but rather for profit. We had that distinction in respect of hospitals, and we have carried forward the same expression in this section 105A. The test as

to whether one of these institutions is public is whether or not it has been in receipt of a grant from either the federal government or a provincial government.
During the last three or four years at budget times we have been receiving large numbers of communications from such institutions across the country asking that this privilege be extended to them. I have been checking with my advisers, and we cannot remember any case brought forward in which this test was not applicable. Institutions which have communicated with us have said: "We meet the same test as hospitals, in that we receive a grant from the public treasury"- either from a province or from the federal government. Hon. members will appreciate that this is a new field which is not easy to control. That is one reason why we are postponing the actual bringing into effect of this amendment until July 1, so that we shall have another couple of months to work out the details of the regulations.
During the course of the year we shall be able to determine whether or not any real hardship is imposed on worth-while charitable institutions of this type because of this provision. If that should be the case, the matter will be considered again.

subtopic: QUESTIONS AS TO INFESTATION OF APHIDS IN SOUTHERN MANITOBA
speechtext:
I should like to make two brief observations. First, what I had to say applied to the test under paragraph (b). I accept the test under paragraph (a), which would confine the benefits of the exemption to institutions that are clearly public in character because of the beneficial work they are seeking to do. Of course that qualification will remain. It is the additional qualification which I submit is entirely too narrow and restrictive.
In the second place, I appreciate that this is a new departure. I think it is a praiseworthy departure, and I hope it will be regarded by the government as only the first step. I ask the parliamentary assistant to give us assurance that this particular aspect of the problem, namely, the possibility of extending exemptions to institutions whose only public assistance is derived from municipal governments, will be given serious study between now and the next session, and that in the light of the experience gained in the administration of the section the matter will be further reviewed.

speechtext:
During the last two decades there has been a tremendous increase in the consumption by our people of so-called creams which were thought to have emanated from the cow but which may be found to have emanated from the coconut tree. I should like to reiterate the statement made many years ago in this house as to how such commodities replace the production of our dairy farms. Ice cream and creams of other kinds are foods of great value, but foods which do not absorb as much of our

Excise Tax Act
Canadian dairy production as we would like. Through you, Mr. Chairman, I want the department to know that I do not want any of these synthetic products imported from other countries to be left out of the category on which excise tax is payable. I want to see the real spirit of the idea behind the bill carried out, namely, that Canadian production of dairy products will be free of this tax. These things which are produced by our friends in the Pacific islands, Nigeria, Colombo, Ceylon and the other parts of the world, and are imported into this country, should pay their share of the tax. These people are willing to pay their fair share of the necessary tax to get their goods into this country. I want you, sir, as the person charged with the responsibility of collecting that excise tax, to see that you carry out your duties to the nth degree so these people will not avoid paying the tax.
I think perhaps, Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary assistant knows that in those mixtures that come down 'to us in the form of valuable food, full of calories and all that sort of thing, there are certain things which have not borne excise tax, which tax is supposed to protect the interests of the farmer members of this assembly, sir, and protect the dairy cow. I am not critical. I merely want to put these observations on the record again, as I did at great length in 1934, 1935, 1936, and every other opportunity I had; because we must protect our Canadian economy and help to protect the dairy cow if we can. It is not her fault, nor is it our fault, that we are in this northern climate. It is not our fault that, although the cow produces 100 pounds of milk, one only gets 5 pounds of butterfat, whereas a pickaninny can climb a tree and collect a palm nut from which he gets 45 per cent fat at very little cost to anyone. In that case Providence provides it.
These oils are sent to our warehouses, put through Canadian processing plants, and the resultant product is something which we, as consumers, think of as a dairy product. It is not a dairy product, it is a product of the miscellaneous nuts and fruits which come from the Pacific islands and the other parts of the world. I have no objection to it at all, but the excise tax is designed to help us get some revenue from the products which come from other countries. I say to you, sir, that there are more gallons, hundredweights, or tons, or any other unit of measure you wish, of this commodity coming into this country than our native cows will ever produce, and it will come in increasing quantities as the days go by. The parliamentary assistant has a duty to perform to those of us in Canada who depend on the

government, in a small way, to collect our dues at the border from these tremendous importations of vegetable oil products from practically all parts of the world. Bring them in, of course, but let them pay their toll.
If it is the opinion of the government that this legislation in some degree helps to protect the producers of butterfat, then go a little further and do some research work to see to what extent that is being accomplished. I am not critical of it, but make sure -I am not talking, Mr. Chairman, to the minister or his deputy just now, I am talkipg to the deputies who are serving under them -that your administration of this particular act is such that it will approximate 100 per cent efficiency. When I pass a bakery shop window and I see a pie with some whipped cream on top, I want to know whether that is whipped cream or whether it is coconut butter made from coconut oil that came from some other part of this terrestrial ball, rather than from the milk cow of Canada. If the truth were known, nine times out of ten that whipped cream that is on top of that pie is not whipped cream at all but whipped coconut oil or some other kind of oil, which found its way into this country and was processed. It was looked after by some big packing house or soap industry, which in turn sold it to that bakery. For what reason? It looked good; it tasted good; and it would stay in the bakeshop window and remain in good condition for many more hours than would the whipped cream from the Canadian cow. When the consumer bought the pie, he thought he was eating a domestic product. In like manner the housewife is deceived when she buys shortening. She thinks she is getting something domestic, and she should know that there is hardly anything domestic in that particular shortening. It all comes from the other countries which I mentioned a moment ago. Why the laws of this country should allow the word "domestic" to be used to that extent, I do not know. Why we should permit the housewives to be fooled by a lot of these products, very often combined with other products, which evade these excise taxes, is something I cannot understand. I am saying to those who serve in that department that they should see to it that these products do not escape the tax. Eight per cent is a miserably small percentage of the whole thing.
In Montreal some years ago I saw one tank steamer loaded with Chinese peanut oil, and she was so heavily laden that they had to lighter the ship because she could not tie up to the dock. This product cost less than three cents a pound, and it was necessary to

lighter that tremendous cargo to get it into Canada. I ask any ordinary farmer to tell me how butterfat can be produced at three, four, five or even ten cents a pound, to compete with products from these other parts of the world, and still permit our Canadian agricultural industry, our Canadian livestock industry, and our Canadian dairy industry to survive. We do not mind competition, but God put us on this North American continent and we have difficulty in pasturing our cattle. We cannot pasture our cattle the year round as is done in some other countries. We must build barns, but in many countries no barns are necessary, and the cattle can remain out the year round.
We cannot do that here. Yet we are here and we are a country by ourselves. Let us take charge and assume responsibility for our country. In these few words I am saying, I know I am getting a little bit away from the point. I know that you, Mr. Chairman, are getting ready to call me to order. I can see your fingers wobbling. I know I am a little bit away from the point, but I am putting this on record with your indulgence, sir, so that these gentlemen under the minister and under his deputy will see that this little excise tax is collected, that this law is carried out, that there will be no evasion or getting away from it. When I go past the next bakeshop window and see that whipped cream on a custard pie I want to know, Mr. Parliamentary Assistant, that it has paid its full excise tax, if it is not whipped cream; and I want to see the farmer protected if it is whipped cream, in order to help in a little way.
As one year succeeds another, I can see the fading-and I will say this in a voice that will be heard-of the dairy industry. That fading is coming about not through any fault of ours but owing to the fact that we in this northern zone and the other zones are backed up with these free trade ideas of all kinds of administrations across Canada. Through all the conferences that are being held at Geneva and what not, with the advent of that day and generation, I gave this warning to the people of Canada: as Geneva proceeds, and as these protections, if you like, proceed-you understand that word; that is why I use it, I do not think it means protection in the full sense of the word as it appears in the Oxford dictionary-this conservation of our livelihood and native industry, call it protection if you will, is not enough to stop what is happening in the universe in the production of these products. They are not synthetic. They are natural products. They will keep coming. But before this bill passes I want those in your department to see to it that there is no evasion, no mixture, no
Railway Act
adulteration, that when it is stated to be whipped cream, it is whipped cream and when it is stated to be a filling of some kind or something else, it has paid its excise tax.

speechtext:
This matter was discussed in committee on May 5, and I do not propose to review or to traverse any of the ground that was covered there. There is, however, one subject that I should like to bring before the committee. As the minister has said, the effect of this amendment to section 262 of the Railway Act is, first, to increase the annual statutory grant commencing April 1, 1951, from $500,000 to $1 million; and second, to

Railway Act
raise the maximum available out of the fund, on order of the board of transport commissioners, from $100,000 to $150,000. There is, however, no change proposed in the bill with regard to the other maximum, namely the 40 per cent.
As I indicated when speaking on the resolution stage of this bill on May 5, there are good reasons why the maximum amount available out of the fund for any one work should be increased from $100,000 to $150,000. The cost of these grade separations and crossing protective works has increased tremendously, and the railways are having their own difficult time with financial problems, so that if there is to be any attack on the problem of level crossings in Canada, we must accept the fact that the railways are not in a position to bear the brunt of the burden. There are also good reasons why, apart from the financial aspect, they should not be called upon to do so. The fact that the problem is growing in its scope and in its intensity is largely attributable to increased highway traffic. I submit that there is good ground for increasing the present 40 per cent maximum. It has been increased in times past. An increase in that percentage is nothing new. It stood at 25 per cent for many years. The reasons that led parliament to increase to 40 per cent this maximum percentage have, I think, grown stronger in the interval since that last increase was made.
Lest any hon. member should think that there is grave danger in raising that maximum, I point out that it is still subject to the orders of the board of transport commissioners. No sum is available out of that fund except on order of the board. Such are the provisions of the Railway Act. All that we are doing, if we increase the 40 per cent maximum, is to say to the board of transport commissioners: If you think the circumstances warrant it, after you have heard the case and reviewed all the evidence, we are not going to impose so low an arbitrary limit on the amount available out of the railway grade crossing fund.
Sir, as I sought to indicate in my remarks on May 5, this fund has had a record of remarkable achievement. It has been a highly commendable piece of remedial legis- ' lation. I do urge that the time has come for a further relaxation of the percentage maximum that now is imposed under section 262. I think in that way we shall be taking a forward step. We shall be contributing toward the expansion in all parts of the country of the desirable work of grade separation and protective works at crossings, and we shall, I am convinced, contribute

to the saving of life and the avoidance of those accidents which have taken many lives and maimed many persons.
It should always be remembered, Mr. Chairman, that there is no money available out of the railway grade crossing fund to assist in the maintenance of crossing works. The railway grade crossing fund is available only to assist in the construction of those protective works on crossings or actual grade separations. That is a further limitation, and when we measure, on the one hand, the necessity of works of the kind we are speaking of here, the great field that still remains for remedial operation of legislation of this kind and of funds of the nature of the railway grade crossing funds, and, on the other hand, the restrictions that still exist even if this percentage maximum were increased, the fact that $150,000 is the maximum amount in any particular case, and the fact that the fund is available only for assistance in construction, not toward maintenance, and in the third place that it is always subject to the orders of the board of transport commissioners, and not one copper comes out of that fund unless the board of transport commissioners is satisfied it ought to come out, and others who are to pay are contributing their share, then it seems to me the case is very strong for the increase in the 40 per cent.
There is one other aspect to this, and I mention it briefly in conclusion, Mr. Chairman. The increase that is being proposed in this bill for any one work from $100,000 to $150,000, with 40 per cent maximum, is going to be very helpful in the case of the large and expensive crossing protective works. But there are many crossing works of a protective nature that do not run into these very big figures. There are many crossings where protective works could be installed to the very great advantage and benefit of the public, where costly works of grade separation are not required. I am thinking particularly of cases of the kind where great local benefit will ensue when I urge that the present percentage maximum of 40 per cent should be increased.
I mention again that in doing so we shall be simply consistent with past history; we shall be simply taking one step forward in this respect, following steps of a similar nature taken in the same direction in the past, in the light of conditions, consistent with those which led to the increase in times past, and which have lately become intensified in their effect.

Mr. Chairman, I am happy to endorse what the hon. member for

Eglinton has had to say. To save time perhaps the minister could reply to both of us at the same time. I have a few specific instances to mention, of which the minister has been well advised. Before proceeding to make some suggestions I should like to put on the record that from my point of view at least for over a quarter of a century the city of Toronto has been pretty well looked after with regard to the amount of money expended out of this fund to eliminate level crossings. Perhaps we have not had favours to the same extent as our friends from Montreal, but we have had certain favours. The occasion was the grade separation for the half million population in the environs of the city of Toronto from Queen street east, to the union station. These benefits were obtained by an organization known as the Toronto Terminals Railway Company, which was set up. But during this quarter of a century there has been a tremendous increase in the population to the east of where the Toronto Terminals Railway Company started in with their great work some twenty odd years ago.
In passing, the deputation which waited on the ministry at that time went from my humble office in the House of Commons, where they gathered their facts together. But the minister did a great job for us at that time. I think the amount was around $22 million, and you could not do the job today for $50 million. Populations grow. I am anxious to impress on the minister and on his department the tremendous growth of the population east of the area which you protected by the grade separation of that day and of that generation.
A new city has arisen in the area east of that, but the old railway line is still there. The level crossings are still there. Mr. Chairman, now that the hon. member for Danforth has referred to his own constituency which, I think, was done properly, I suggest all hon. members should recognize the problems found in large industrial areas and the thickly populated cities in the matter of having proper facilities for grade crossing purposes, always keeping in mind the object of saving life and moving traffic more expeditiously.
I made reference to this same matter the other day when the bill was in resolution

stage, and I would refer to it again now, developing somewhat further the thoughts I presented at that time. I hope that, like the hon. member for Danforth, I may be pardoned if my remarks are brought down to the constituency level. I do this because I believe what I have in mind must apply equally well to many other sections in Canada.
In Manitoba the railways concentrate largely in an area not far from the city of Winnipeg, particularly on the north side of the Assiniboine river. Leading out to Portage la Prairie we have the two main lines of the national railways, both the C.P.R. and the C.N.R. The topography is such that they approach the city from one side and go out the other. The highway crosses both those railways on each side of the city, and these are level crossings. They are hazardous because there is no adequate warning of the approach of trains. On one side we find an electrical stop gate, which works very well; but on the other side, where both railways are criss-crossing the highway, there is no such protection. In fact, the only protection afforded is an ordinary stop sign.
This may be warning enough, in one sense; but it has the effect, if the sign is properly recognized, of stopping all the traffic which comes along. Traffic for miles back may be affected by that stop sign, and it does not get away as quickly as it should when, in fact, there may be no train for miles back. My suggestion is that in the interests of the better movement of traffic something more should be done by means of this grade crossing fund to stop traffic when trains are approaching and not to stop it when there are no trains within some considerable distance.
The other feature I have in mind, one which no doubt affects many other hon. members, is that in this instance the railways are crossing what will be our trans-Canada highway, or what is likely to be recognized as such. So that in the end, while naturally the local municipalities are interested in having adequate crossings, the whole of the province- indeed the whole of the country-is interested in having there some facilities which will make traffic easier and safer. This brings in a new principle in connection with the grade crossings because now the trans-Canada highway is involved. My submission is that in those cases where the railroad crosses the trans-Canada highway, a highway which will be utilized by people from all over the country, the local municipalities should not be required to pay as large a proportion of the cost of any facilities provided as might be paid in other cases. Where it is in the national interest that the crossing should be

eliminated more of the cost should come from federal sources as well as from the province, and not so much from the municipality.
I have no idea of the cost of these things and in the instance I have in mind I am not suggesting a subway or anything like that. I have watched the operation of these electrical signals and I think that would be quite adequate. I submit that this is a matter of considerable importance and I hope it will not be overlooked when we are laying plans for the protection of travellers on our highways and our railroads.

Mr. Chairman, like those who have gone before me I have a personal interest to serve when I speak about something in the city in which I live. But I first want to make a suggestion which will not cost the government any money. This is something I have been advocating for a number of years. I refer to the distinction in law which obtains in the United States and in Canada. I am not speaking now so much of the monetary losses that might be suffered by any government or railroad or person; I am speaking of the loss of human life, I am speaking of the injuries to human beings which occur when there is an argument between a railroad engine and a truck or motorcar at a level crossing.
Unless it has been changed recently the general law prevailing in the United States is that of stop, look and listen, while in Canada we leave out the word "stop". The overriding rule of law here is simply look and listen. There are many lawsuits because of accidents at crossing and the usual story is that the whistle was not heard or the train seen because of a bank along the side and that kind of thing. I am not concerned so much about that because anyone who has spoken to a Canadian Pacific or Canadian National engineer no doubt has been told of instances where motorcars have crashed right into the side of a train which was moving across a level crossing. Those are not isolated cases. On the line of railroad with which 1 am familiar I know that such a thing, hard as it is to believe, has happened again and again.
I do not know under what authority it is, but in the provinces there are laws that vehicles licensed to carry passengers must stop at grade crossings. Trucks stop at grade crossings, and so do the busses carrying school children which are now used in the new scheme of getting children to larger schools. I have never heard from anyone any real reason why we should not have the general rule of stop, look and listen. I repeat that I am not talking about what it may cost the railroad or the man who is injured; I am
Railway Act
referring to the injuries which often result in death and which could be almost eliminated if the people could be persuaded to obey that rule. I think they would, once they knew it was a general rule, although it might take time.
If a person stops at a railroad crossing he is likely to look and listen. We would thus do away with the great majority of fatal accidents at level crossings. I am not expecting an immediate answer but I do ask the minister and those associated with him to give this matter their consideration. I intend to go on now to speak about the need for a subway in Calgary, but first I should like to ask the minister if the word "cost" as used in the amendment would cover the damages payable to the occupiers of adjoining properties?

Mr. Chairman, while we are discussing this section there is one point I should like to mention. In doing so I recognize it involves the type of case where there is a joint interest between the dominion government and the provincial government concerned as to the particular problem. As mentioned by the member who has just spoken, there are many cases where engineers report automobiles driving right into the side of the engine or other part of the train, and there almost seems to be evidence that there was no regard for the fact that there was a track there. I think those who travel a great deal on the highways in any part of Canada know that many roads passing through wooded areas or where there is a rise and fall in the ground approach rail lines with very little advance notice that there is a track there. I do not care how careful a driver is. At the speeds now permitted by the law on open country highways a car approaches a railroad level crossing so fast that often it will be almost on the track before the driver is aware that the crossing is there.
Immediately the answer occurs to one's mind that there are signs on the highways indicating the presence of railway crossings. It is to the question of those very signs that I am directing my remarks because they are a part of the problem of protecting such crossings. Most of them are still in the same

places that they were when cars travelled about half the speed they do today. All too often the sign indicating the presence of a railroad crossing is sufficiently close to the crossing itself that, travelling even within the maximum legal speed limit, there is scarcely time for the brakes to operate, particularly if the road surface is wet.
I earnestly suggest to the minister that consideration be given throughout the whole country in co-operation with provincial highway departments to the placing of the signs warning of railway crossings far enough back so that where there is a curve in a highway, a dip or anything of that kind, or in fact under any circumstances, the careful car driver will have plenty of warning that he is approaching a railway crossing. I have seen several crossings on highways in different parts of the country where the most careful driver really did not have adequate warning that he was about to go over a railway track. Perhaps it may be at the lower part of a depression where, with a wet hardsurfaced road, he will have great difficulty in bringing his car to a stop, if there is any possibility of doing so at all. I am simply taking the discussion on this section as an opportunity to urge the most careful and the earliest possible discussion of this subject with the highway department of each province with the idea of assuring the general practice that such warning signals are well back from the crossing in order to warn drivers of the fact that they will soon be crossing a railway track.

Mr. Chairman, there are one or two suggestions I should like to make to the minister on this subject having to do with section 1, the sum of $150,000 and the 40 per cent maximum. That will mean that a grade separation costing $266,667 will draw a maximum of $150,000 from the fund. Anything over that will have to be paid entirely by the railway company and the municipality. Under modern conditions of construction I am afraid we are going to find that grade separations, particularly on densely travelled highways, need a great deal more excavation. Grades, either for bridges or for subways, have to be much more gradual now than formerly because of the higher speed of traffic, and consequently the excavation and frontage used for grade separation necessarily are much greater. Therefore I suggest that consideration should be given to removing the maximum of $150,000, and letting the provision be 40 per cent of the over-all cost. I know of one or two grade separations which are pressing at the moment. I have talked to engineers about one of them, and have been informed that the cost will be in the

neighbourhood of $350,000. Under the present regulations this would mean that the whole amount over $266,667 would have to be provided by the railway and the municipality, which would act as a deterrent to the immediate commencement of the work on the grade crossing in question.
Another suggestion I have for the minister's consideration is this. The province of Ontario has under consideration a program of new road construction, all of which covers the four-lane highways with a separation between lanes, restricted entrance to the highway from side roads, and which involves an expenditure of about $500 million. That will not be spent this year or next year, but that is the program that has been laid out. I suggest to this house that, in view of the tremendous increase in traffic and the enormous amount of new highway construction in the United States, this expenditure is necessary if we are going to provide arterial highways of a size to take care of the volume of traffic which will be debouched into Ontario from the major points of contact with the new United States highways. When grade separation is undertaken on these new roads I would suggest, therefore, that instead of the limit being 40 per cent of the total cost, it should be increased to 50 per cent or 60 per cent. If these new major trunk arteries are constructed, and for the sake of economy during the initial construction they are built with level crossings, the volume of traffic will build up to such an extent that grade separation will later become an absolute necessity, and the cost of dealing with it will be immeasurably greater than if it were undertaken at the time the road is constructed. I suggest it is a matter of true economy to have these roads constructed, wherever possible, with grade separation.
I come to one other point, and that is that I believe the new sections of the trans-Canada highway particularly should be constructed with the grades separated, and the cost of the work should be considered as an item of expense directly attributable to the highway construction. In my constituency there is a condition which exists in that warning signals, wigwags, bells, lights and other sound signals are frequently activated by freight trains, which are either shunting in one end of the yard or awaiting entry into the major freight yard. This condition has two evil effects. As a matter of fact, the board of transport commissioners did a lot of work with the C.P.R. in that connection, and at one crossing in particular, namely, the Dundas street crossing near Islington a remedy has been found. When a wigwag works because a train is standing there waiting to get into the yard, those people who habitually use that crossing become careless. There is a tendency to 55946-152
Railway Act
disregard the signal, because frequently the wigwag is working for a train which has been standing on that part of the track which activates the signal for periods of fifteen to twenty minutes. While I do not know of any specific accident that has taken place because of that condition, it is extremely dangerous. Frequently I have seen motorists cross the track when the wigwag was working without even glancing up to see whether there was a train coming. It is rather like calling "wolf, wolf", and eventually there will be a wolf.
I do not believe the compulsory stop sign is a workable law. I understand that the compulsory stop sign is used in the province of Quebec, but not in the province of Ontario. It is seldom obeyed in those provinces which have that law, and I feel it is possibly not a wise provision because it is merely written into the statute books, and then the law falls into disrepute. I believe that completes what I have to say on this question at the moment, Mr. Chairman, but I want to reiterate what I said before, because the evidence has shown that over 80 per cent of the accidents which have taken place in the last five years in Canada have taken place at unprotected country crossings where the whistle was sounded as a warning. In the urban sections where crossings were protected by wigwags, lights, or other sound signals, the accident incidence has greatly diminished.
I just want to bring that point out because this abolition of the whistle sounding at certain level crossings in my own constituency has definitely and specifically not resulted in any increase in accidents at those level crossings. The board of transport commissioners have insisted that where the whistle was done away with the automatic electric signal should be installed. The net result is that these crossings have a much better record over the past year than they had prior to the installation of the wigwag.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lionel Chevrier (Minisler of Transport) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 153, to amend the Aeronautics Act.
He said: This bill to amend the Aeronautics Act does not involve any basic changes in government authority or in the policy which the government has pursued in the field of aviation. Experience in the administration of the act during the period of rapid growth of commercial civil aviation since the end of the recent war has, however, brought to light a number of lesser changes and adjustments which if made will clarify the intent of the act and make it possible for the civil aviation authorities to avoid confusion in interpretation and to act with that degree of flexibility which rapid changes in flying require.
It is not necessary at this stage to review all these lesser amendments in detail since they are fully explained in the notes accompanying the bill. I will, however, mention a few of the more important in order to give the house some indication of the main points as well as the general nature and type of the changes proposed.
Part I of the Aeronautics Act represents the original framework of law approved by parliament for the development and regulation of civil aviation shortly after the first world war. It relates to the powers and duties of the government and the minister and, in consequence, of that part of the Department of Transport which deals with air matters and is concerned primarily with technical control; that is, such matters as airport and airway development and technical and safety regulation of all civil flying. It also concerns certain references to national defence in view of the fact that the civil aviation machinery was originally set up within a military framework.
Part II of the act, which was added at a later stage in 1944, provides for the economic supervision and regulation of commercial aviation in such matters as licensing, interrelationships, fares and rates, and describes the powers of the government, the minister, and the air transport board in this field.

Certain of the amendments in this bill are designed to clarify the relationship between parts I and II by eliminating possible duplication in coverage between the two sections. References to national defence are corrected or eliminated as well, in view of the fact that the necessary coverage in this field is now provided elsewhere.
Another point of some importance relates to jurisdiction over Canadian aircraft or Canadian air services operating outside the territorial limits of Canada. It is obviously desirable that aircraft of Canadian registry and Canadian commercial air services should observe adequate technical and safety requirements when flying outside the country as well as within Canada; and further, that in the general field of regulation of routes, economic policies, fares to be charged and similar matters, Canadian carriers should have some responsibility to the Canadian authorities. This is not a matter of maintaining a pattern for Canadian operations abroad that is consistent with the domestic pattern, but is a matter also of observing the commitments we have undertaken in relation to other governments under the international civil aviation convention and under various bilateral air agreements to which the Canadian government is a party. In the multilateral convention and the bilateral agreements, governments have assumed certain responsibilities with regard to the actions of their own aircraft and commercial air services when in the territories of other countries. In order to carry out these international commitments, the government's jurisdiction over Canadian aircraft and Canadian air services must not only apply within the bounds of Canada but should be general. The bill, therefore, proposes changes in both part I and part II which will satisfy these objectives.
The responsibility for the economic supervision and regulation of commercial air services in Canada is based upon the definition of a commercial air service as an operation for hire or reward. In view of certain doubts that have been cast upon the meaning of hire and reward in this context, a definition of this phrase which will eliminate doubt as to the general definition of a commercial air service is included in this bill.
The sections in both part I and part II of the act which deal with the imposition of penalties for violation of the law have been changed to make them more like similar provisions in other federal statutes, and to provide for somewhat stiffer penalties. This is considered desirable in view of the fact that existing penalties have been found to lack sufficient deterrent value to combat the

seriousness of the offences committed. Fewer violations would occur and fewer prosecutions would be necessary if penalties imposed were somewhat more severe.
Part II of the act grants general jurisdiction over commercial air services, but the new bill would exempt military aircraft from this jurisdiction since these should not be put in the same category generally as commercial air services, even though upon occasion, for example in the air .survey field, certain revenue may be received by the R.C.A.F. for the use of military aircraft on federal government work.
The act presently requires the air transport board to make a finding of public convenience and necessity in regard to the establishment of any scheduled air service. One of the proposed amendments will permit the board to waive this requirement in the case of foreign scheduled air services since provision for these services is made on the basis of a government decision through bilateral agreements between Canada and other nations. The additional requirement that the air transport board subsequently find public convenience and necessity before granting a licence to such foreign carrier is inconsistent with the carrying out of the obligations assumed by the government in these bilateral air agreements.
It is also proposed to change somewhat the powers of the air transport board with regard to investigation of possible violations of the law and to its powers to take corrective action without waiting on formal complaints in these matters. This should simplify and make more expeditious the remedying of difficulties.
As I stated above, the other charges in the bill are of a relatively minor nature and need not be detailed at this time. It is my intention, if the house approves, to refer the bill for detailed examination at the committee stage to the parliamentary committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

It was the declared government policy that the railroads had to get out of the air business.
Some of us fought this in the house strenuously. We pointed out that Canadian Pacific Air Lines were flying a route from Vancouver and Edmonton to the Yukon and giving excellent service; also a route along the north shore of the St. Lawrence. We pointed out that there was no one to take over those services. But in spite of all that, the minister repeated time and again that he was going to put the railroads out of the aviation business.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendments that are before us are amendments that are primarily intended to expand the functions and responsibilities of the board set up by the Aeronautics Act. At the time the amendments to this act were introduced in 1944, there was a great deal of discussion in regard to the structure of the board itself, as to the measure of actual control over the board which the minister was called upon to exercise. It was pointed out that the board would not be a judicial or semi-judicial body exercising independent authority in the manner of the civil aviation board in the United

Aeronautics Act
States, or of other boards of that type. The board, in fact, was really an agency which carried out its functions with the authority and under the direction of the minister.
Many of the statements made at that time, which expressed concern about the possibility of this board merely becoming an instrument of ministerial authority, have not been realized. They have not been realized, not because the dangers inherent in the act were not there, but rather because the board has not carried out the functions which it was intended to carry out at the time it was created by these earlier amendments.
My remarks tonight are directed particularly to my own conviction that the time has come for us to realize that civil aviation in this country has been stifled, and that it has not been assisted by the government in advancing in the way that it should have been. I believe that this is the appropriate time to make certain suggestions, which I do in all earnestness, in the hope that with the amendments which are before us the original purpose of this board, no matter whether or not it was properly planned in the first place, will be carried out in future proposals, to the extent of advancing in every way possible the development of civil aviation in this country and outside of it by Canadian aircraft and air crews.
I did begin to make some comments on this subject on an earlier occasion when we were discussing the estimates. Now that the bill is before us, perhaps I could best continue those remarks. Canada had demonstrated that there is something in the life of our people, something in the way in which we adapt ourselves to great spaces, something in the vitality of our people that comes from the sort of country in which we were born or in which we have come to live, that gives us a special opportunity of leading the whole world in this new type of transportation. Our sights should be high. We should be looking upward all the time we discuss civil aviation. In the first world war, in a completely new means of locomotion and in an entirely new type of warfare, young Canadians showed that they had qualities second to none in the whole world. Not simply to clarify military history but simply to leave the evidence as a permanent record of that fact before our people, it is well for us to recall from time to time that the top pilots of the fighter squadrons of the world were Canadians. It is a good thing for young Canadians today to remember men like Billy Bishop, Raymond Collishaw, Billy Barker and a number of other men who followed

close to them, and whose names will forever be recorded on the pages of Canadian history. It was a gallant company.
These men did not let their interests in aviation end with the war. Many of them went out into new and unorganized fields, and created great civil aviation developments here in this country. Men who had taken their part in that war, young men like MacLaren, who in a few months rose to be the sixth ranking pilot in the allied air forces, took their place in civil aviation, along with Roy Brown, Punch Dickens, Wop May, Gilbert McConachie, whose names are all associated with the development of the air routes of this country. Canadians even today hardly realize the extent to which we were pioneers in air development.
The great Eldorado radium mine which played its part in the closing military history of this last war was discovered from the air from a plane flown by Punch Dickens. The great mineral developments of northern Manitoba were actually spotted from the air. Some of the great new developments in northern Ontario and northern Quebec were first seen from exploring aircraft. Aircraft played an enormous part in the discovery of the almost limitless iron resources of Quebec and Labrador. No country in the world has benefited more in a positive and measurable way than has this country from the employment of aircraft in the hands of young and vigorous men of vision and of energy who were prepared to open out new routes and new fields of endeavour.
Then in this last world war once again Canadians demonstrated those same unique qualities. There are hon. members in this house who took their full share in the glorious record of the R.C.A.F. We ended that war with the greatest pool of trained pilots, trained aircrew and trained technicians per capita of any country in the world. We had everything wide open to us. The United States was undoubtedly in the most favoured position, with their enormous numbers of trained men and women and their enormous productive capacity. But next to them, we certainly were in a position to go out and to take the lead in this new means of transport. Whether or not the amendments to the Aeronautics Act of 1944 were well conceived, at least it can be said that in setting up the air transport board at that time and in creating certain authority in the hands of that board, it was quite obviously intended that this, with the guidance of the minister, should be for the purpose of taking advantage of those very opportunities to which I have referred and those opportunities which were so clearly in the minds of our people at that

time with all the activities that were going on in connection with the commonwealth air training program in this country.
Those opportunities have not been developed as they should have been developed.
I say this now not for the purpose of criticizing what is past but with the hope that we shall recognize the enormous opportunities we have; that, with whatever amendments are made, the original intention of the air transport board will be carried out; and that we shall as a nation extend our air activities so that we may occupy in this new means of transport that position of leadership which our own native qualifications as a people make possible and which geography has offered to us with very special advantages.
Every young Canadian should be trained to look at the world by examining the circular globe instead of a flat map. If they get their idea of geography with a clear impression of our extraordinary advantages in air transportation, perhaps our people will realize the extent to which we have opportunities open to no other nation in the world. The shortest routes from New York or Chicago to Tokyo, to any great city of China, to Melbourne or to any of the cities of the east, lie through Canada. The shortest routes to London, to Paris, to Rome, to Berlin-yes, and to Moscow-are through Canada. East and west, geography has placed us on the main air routes of the world. We should be putting all the energy and initiative that we possess into the development of air routes out to those distant points-to South Africa, to South America and to every part of the world -so that Canadian aircraft may be known in every great airport where the commerce of the air moves back and forth.
This is no uncertain dream. This is no loosely optimistic expression of hope. This is something that can be done. We have seen how other people have done it. Holland, a tiny country across which fast aircraft can travel in from an hour to an hour and a half, ended the war during which it had been occupied by the forces of Germany with no aircraft of their own, and with relatively few trained pilots. Today they have a company which is the third air transport system in the world. The Dutch KLM is today flying air routes of 75,000 miles as against total air routes under the largest Canadian transport organization, Trans-Canada Air Lines, of 16,000 miles. The thing which should make every Canadian think today is the fact that a large part of the expansion of those activities of KLM was carried out by young Canadians, because a large percentage of the pilots and technicians of KLM, which is known in every great airport of the world, are Canadians 55946-153
Aeronautics Act
who went there to use the special skill they had gained during the war or in the days immediately after. Everything that we do as members of parliament should, I believe, be for the purpose of unleashing the unbounded energy of our vigorous people in this special type of transportation for which we are so unusually qualified. What we should avoid, what we should fight against in every way we can, is anything of a restrictive nature which denies to young men and women of vigour and of vision the opportunity to extend the development of this great transportation system which we can build. For that reason we should examine more carefully what the functions were that the air transport board was supposed to carry out, and what has actually happened since that time.
The amendments now before us are intended to increase the opportunity of the board to do certain things which will be to the advantage of civil aviation in this country. It is intended to extend the power of the board:
To undertake, and to co-operate with persons undertaking, such products, technical research, study or investigation as in his opinion-
-that is the minister's opinion-
-will promote the development of aeronautics in Canada.
It is also intended to extend the power of the board:
To take such action as may be necessary to secure,
. . . rights ... in international air traffic.
It is also intended to extend the power of the board:
To investigate, examine and report on the operation and development of commercial air services within or partly within Canada or the limits of the territorial waters of Canada.
It is also intended to extend the authority of the board to recommend regulations which will be adopted by the government for the control or operation of aircraft registered in Canada wherever such aircraft may be. There are a number of other amendments to this act which come in the early part of the bill now before us. That sounds very well; naturally hon. members will feel that the extension of these opportunities will be of advantage to the board. But it would be well for all of us to remember that the board has not been exercising the functions which it was intended to exercise. One of the reasons for that became fully apparent in the evidence which was given recently before the committee on railways and shipping, where evidence was taken in regard to the activities of the Trans-Canada Air Lines. Just as an example of what I mean I would recall that

Aeronautics Act
when we were seeking to ascertain the manner in which Trans-Canada Air Lines opened up new routes, we learned that Trans-Canada Air Lines did not decide what new routes would be taken. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), not the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), made it quite clear that the decision in regard to new routes was under his direction, and in one of the typically forceful expressions that he is given to making from time to time he left no doubt about it that that was his responsibility.

speechtext: While I am a member of the committee on railways and shipping, I was not present on the occasion to which my hon. friend refers, but the information I have- I wish my hon. friend had the evidence-is that the Minister of Trade and Commerce did not make that statement. subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I quite agree with the minister that he said it was the responsibility of the government, and I shall be very happy to make the exact reference to the evidence, but I point out that in explaining the way it was done the Minister of Trade and Commerce left no doubt whatever that he was the one whose views would be considered in that respect. After all, that is the very point I wish to make. We have this extraordinary situation, and I did mention it the other night. Actually I have been hopeful that the government would take some action in regard to this unusual situation. The Trans-Canada Air Lines is not an independent publicly-owned organization. The Trans-Canada Air Lines is a fully-owned subsidiary of the Canadian National Railways. It is an organization in which the total holding of securities is in the hands of the Canadian National Railways.
To a very large extent the directors of the two organizations are the same men. Yet we have the situation that while the parent organization, the Canadian National Railways, is under the ministerial responsibility of the Minister of Transport, the wholly-owned subsidiary, the Trans-Canada Air Lines, is under the Minister of Trade and Commerce. That is not an argument as to the relative merits of the Minister of Transport or the Minister of Trade and Commerce. We, after all, are dealing with an act of parliament, a bill which is presented to us for consideration, which does not deal with individuals as individuals, but establishes a legal structure under which any minister, whoever he may be from time to time, must carry out the responsibilities assigned by that statute.
Under this bill now before us a board is set up which has the supervising authority

over civil aviation. That board is under the Minister of Transport. That board is charged with the responsibility of investigating new routes, carrying out investigations and explorations for the purpose of extending the activities of our air services, not merely the chosen instrument, Trans-Canada Air Lines, but all air services; and nevertheless you have the situation that the minister in charge of Trans-Canada Air Lines, the chosen instrument in the domestic field and externally, is under the Minister of Trade and Commerce; whereas the Minister of Transport is not only the minister responsible for the parent organization, the Canadian National Railways, but is also the minister under whose authority the air transport board is bound to act, under the wording of this statute.
That can only cause confusion; that can only cause unnecessary duplication of discussion and duplication of representation, because you have the same men dealing with the Canadian National Railways on the one hand going to the Minister of Transport about their problems in relation to the railways, and incidentally their problems in relation to their subsidiary, Trans-Canada Air Lines, and you have the same men, or very largely the same men, called upon to go to another minister to discuss the problems of Trans-Canada Air Lines, the subsidiary, in regard to the very subject matter that by the Aeronautics Act is placed under the board, and the supervision of the minister in relation to that board.
I am convinced that part of the reason Canada has not extended its air activities as it should lies in the frustration created by this severance of responsibility. Whether it be the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) or whether it be the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), I am satisfied that good business sense suggests that it should be the same minister dealing with these two organizations which are interrelated in their legal structure, two organizations which very largely have the same directors, two organizations in which the officials perform in a number of cases the same functions. These two organizations should be brought under the same minister, whoever that minister may be.
Then if we do that, and the same minister in turn is the minister responsible for the activities of the air transport board, you have an integrated organization which can direct all its activities to the development and the extension of civil air services in this country. I would of course emphasize the fact that it is civil air services we are speaking
*i i

about, because the military services are under the Department of National Defence, outside *the field of this discussion.
It is not only in the air services out to the distant points of the world that we have failed to take advantage of the great opportunities we possess; it is also right here in our own country. Look at the air map. Look at the routes, and you will see that we have a single trunk line across the country. We have only a few lines running north and south-very few. We have none of those feeder services which today are an essential part of the full development of any great trunk system of air transportation.
Do not let anyone try to tell the Canadian people that we have not opportunities- great opportunities-for feeder services here in this country that we are not using today. Look at the British isles, and see how small they are when compared with the size of this country. Yet they have feeder lines running out from the large airports at London and Glasgow and all the other cities of England, Scotland, Ireland and Wales. Those lines not only supply a service to the people in those communities who wish to fly only short distances, when compared with our distances here, but they also provide additional passengers for the trunk routes flying to different parts of the world.
In Ontario and Quebec today there are well over eight million people; that is a substantial population. It is a population that is fairly well concentrated in those two provinces. There are tremendous opportunities for feeder lines in connection with the smaller cities, and to the airports which already exist as a carry-over from the war. Applications have been made for opportunities to operate those feeder lines. Such feeder lines would not only give a convenient service to those municipalities, and a new service to them, but they would feed passengers to Trans-Canada Air Lines and other trunk services as well.
The same is true in all of Canada. There are places where short runs are being made, and being made successfully. For instance, in the maritime provinces we find Maritime Central Airways.

speechtext: The best feeder line in Canada.

speechtext:
I was just going to say that it is one of the most successful, if not the most successful feeder line in Canada, operating south to Fredericton and Moncton, and over to what we are told is the most beautiful city in Canada, the city of Charlottetown. It gives a type of service which not only affords an advantage to the various places it serves but also brings large numbers of 55946-153i
Aeronautics Act
passengers to Moncton to get aboard the Trans-Canada Air Lines service going both ways.
This should be encouraged. It should be an openly declared policy that private feeder lines will be encouraged where they apply. There should be no dog-in-the-manger attitude, that routes which cannot be operated by Trans-Canada Air Lines will not be operated at all. I hope no statement will be made based upon the question of the extent to which formal applications have gone. I am sure those associated with the air transport board are>
well informed in regard to those companies which have sought to operate these feeder services. But in most cases they were told that as a matter of policy it was not likely that they were going to be able to get ahead with that service. And for that very reason the formal procedure may never have been carried past that point. We have in this country, right across Canada, a number of organizations which are ready to carry out feeder services of this type in a way which would be helpful not only to the country as a whole but also to Trans-Canada Air Lines and to Canadian Pacific Air Lines on those main routes which they operate.
Although I do personally believe that the air transport board is wrongly constituted, and although I believe that it should be a semi-judicial body like the civil aeronautics board in Washington, not under the direct authority or direct instruction of a minister, but rather as an independent body passing judgment on applications with an even measure of consideration for all applicants, whether they be public or private organizations, nevertheless I recognize that the question of the constitution of the board is not actually before us in connection with these amendments. Therefore I leave the matter there.
However, I do raise these questions now, because I believe that this is the time, when we have before us these amendments extending the responsibilities of the air transport board, to say we believe that Canada can lead the whole world in developing this new type of transportation, if only opportunities will be thrown wide open to all who can use their knowledge and initiative in giving a service of this kind.
I would hope that, far from taking in a sense of criticism these remarks about the division of authority between ministers, the government would accept these suggestions as helpful, and that it will realize that we can go far ahead of the point we have reached if we are prepared to streamline these governmental services in every way, and bring the

Aeronautics Act
functions of the air transport board, the government air service, and all other organizations of that type under one minister and under one board-and then, in doing that, to have a declared policy of wide-open development of air services in this country.
We are not now arguing as to the merits or demerits of the chosen instrument of policy. The people of this country have accepted the fact that there should be a chosen instrument, the Trans-Canada Air Lines. But with the acceptance of that policy there should also be an insistence that because a chosen instrument has been set up the desires to advance the interests of that chosen instrument should not be a deterrent to the development of private enterprise in the way of feeder lines or trunk lines where such trunk lines will be to the advantage of this country.
I hope that, with these widened opportunities, with the increased measure of authority contemplated by the government, the government will now declare that we are going to extend air development in Canada in every way we can so that every community which can be served by air transportation will be served and that the aircraft of Canada will fly to every great airport throughout the world where air routes can be developed to the advantage of this country and to the extension of our commercial services.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say just a few words which will be addressed to the points made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) at the beginning of his remarks. I should like to echo what the leader of the opposition said as to the challenge and opportunity which is afforded to us by this new and wonderful means of transportation. A year ago I happened to be at Gander airport. One could not be there for very long, no matter how little one liked flying, however pedestrian one was by nature, without his imagination being kindled by finding there in a rather remote part of Newfoundland what could not be described otherwise than as one of the great crossroads of the world*
As the leader of the opposition has already indicated, in that great station there you will find offices of the Dutch air lines, the French, the British, the United States and many others. You meet every kind of people. There I met a journalist who said he could make a living just writing stories about the variety of people who come through that airport. I could certainly believe him after seeing those whom I saw there at that time.
Another point I should like to make is the aptitude of our own men for flying. I remember talking to a British air official early in 
the last war who mentioned some things which interested me a good deal. First of all he stressed the fact that our men excelled in the air. He said, "You know, your boys seem to have some special advantages. I think driving motorcars along your long straight roads has given them a sense of space and distance which perhaps the young men in England do not get." Then he said another interesting thing. "Every Canadian seems to be not only at home with engines but to be always prepared to rely on his engine. When he gets into a plane he seems to think that the engine is going to do everything he wants it to. Canadians have this feeling far more than our own young Englishmen." However, let no one suggest for a moment that the English flying men do not also excel.
There is another thing that comes back to me from the first war. I was at Salisbury plains in the autumn of 1914. All those who were there will remember those strange monuments at Stonehenge, but there were also other monuments there. A great deal of pioneer flying took place at that point and there were many monuments dedicated to the memory of officers killed while flying. One could not help but feel he was witnessing the evidence of sacrifices made by the pioneers. Many of the men who flew in this war felt that they would not have left the ground in the machines flown in 1914. At that time their only offensive weapon was a rifle, and many of them made what use they could of it as such. For photographic work they just took up an ordinary camera and used it over the side of the plane.
I had not intended to speak but the words of the leader of the opposition brought these things back to my mind and I just wanted to echo what he had said. I must confess that I hate flying. Every time I step out of a plane I do so with relief. But nevertheless when I see an airport like Gander, which in a real sense is one of the crossroads of the world, I cannot help but feel how wonderful an opportunity and challenge this new means of transportation offers to this country.
