speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall speak briefly as one who did a fair amount of bush flying before the war. The debt of gratitude that this country owes to those bush pilots can never be adequately understood or repaid. To give you an example of the importance of the job they did in one or two years before the war may I say that the tonnage of freight moved by air from Osisko lake-now renamed Lac Tr6moy-near the great mining centre of Noranda for a considerable period exceeded the tonnage of freight being shipped from the airport then serving New York, which was the

Newark airport. Almost every fifteen minutes an aircraft came in or took off at that great mining area.
The aeroplane built northern Quebec. Those pioneers who flew what they contemptuously called "crates" developed the great extension of the pre-Cambrian shield which some of us think starts at Porcupine and goes right through to Bourlamaque and the great Sullivan area in Quebec. That area is just beginning to reach its maximum development, and I venture to say it is richer in the variety of minerals than any other area in the world.
I shall never forget the first time I flew away from that dock in an old Stinson plane. We flew in the first boiler sent to one of the mines in the Siscoe area. Not only did we fly the boiler, we also flew another most important part of a mining company's assets, the first cook. The cook had a small child and the only place to put the child in the aeroplane was in the fire box of the boiler. That is how the first boiler and the first cook left that lakeside aerodrome and were flown to a mine which has subsequently developed into quite a gold producer. These are the stories-and that is not a particularly good one-of the twenties and the early thirties. We must remember that the great Noranda mine was only brought to fruition about 1926 although the ore body had been known for some time before. That coincided with the development of the area which was quite impossible without the aeroplane. Now I believe there are very few aircraft leaving that base because of the fact that there are roads and there is a railway. The important part is that the policy of the present and the previous administrations has been so discouraging to the prospecting industry that speculative prospecting has almost ceased to exist. True, there are the big companies.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I merely wanted to point that out because as to the Aeronautics Act, about which I am speaking at the moment, I have on frequent occasions in the house taken issue with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) on the policy of a chosen instrument. I took issue with him in the beginning when he wished to divorce air lines completely from the railway companies. Fortunately he and the government have changed their minds in that regard. He took the position he did
Aeronautics Act
because it was not the policy of the United States to have air lines and railway companies working together. Our conditions and problems in air transport are completely different from those of the United States. It is a most important thing to have the railway companies and the air lines working in cooperation rather than in opposition.
I merely want to add my remarks to those of my leader. Canada has led the world by flying where nobody else could fly. The strange native ability of the Canadian to take to the air is a phenomenon which I do not think the post-war generation fully understands. The problems we face today in the development of our north country, that great part of our country which is not suitable for either agriculture or forestry, depend for their solution on the aeroplane. As I have said, we have seen the gradual shrinkage of the small independent operation caused by policies which I have mentioned but which I will not go into in more detail. I suggest to the minister that our future depends on producing the things which the world must have, metals, the produce of the mines. Unless we have a more liberal-with a small 1-policy as to aviation we are not going to carry on the development of our country in the way that the pioneers developed it before the war.
I should like to say a word as to KLM. KLM, largely officered by Canadians, is a prosperous, profitable organization. In this Canadian nation there must be, Mr. Speaker, a genius for flying which makes it possible to fly not only to inaccessible but also to accessible places under great competition, and to do so commercially and profitably.

speechtext:
I have listened with keen interest to the debate which has taken place on the Aeronautics Act, both this afternoon and this evening, and I think that some good will be derived from the discussion. I am at a loss to understand some of the statements, which I want to deal with generally, and in some cases in detail. For instance, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) says that we are not going far enough; we should expand air services across Canada and internationally. The member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins) says we should go slowly, because it is going to cost a tremendous amount of money. I shall deal with that a little later. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) smiles and laughs, but that is his privilege. Let me tell him that the policy of the opposition thus far has been to complain bitterly about government expenditure. The policy of the opposition, in this session at least, has been that we are spending tremendous sums of money, and I presume that if we are to do all the things the opposition wants us to do we cannot do them without the expenditure of funds. In other words, you cannot have all these advantages that many of us would like to have without a considerable cost to the taxpayers of Canada.
I should like to put on Hansard a brief statement of the development of the Aeronautics Act, before dealing with the criticisms and suggestions that were made.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Why did the minister not do that before so that we could deal with it in debate?

In reply to the criticisms made by the opposition. I was going on to say that the Aeronautics Act, which was passed in 1919, dealt generally with the powers and the duties of the minister. Then in 1944 the act was amended and divided into three parts. The first part was substantially the act of 1919; the second part established the air transport board and gave authority, under the minister, to license commercial air services and regulate them; and the functions and powers of the board are

set out more particularly in that part. Part III of the act dealt purely with technical matters regarding the tabling of regulations and the superannuation provision. I make that general statement, because I think it might serve some purpose in the remarks I have to make in answer to some of the charges that were made against the government.
The leader of the opposition and the member for Vancouver-Quadra resumed an old . feud which they have with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe).

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I have not any feud at all.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: They state that the responsibility for T.C.A. should be with the Minister of Transport and not with the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The leader of the opposition made representations the other evening, and again tonight, that T.C.A. should be responsible to the same minister as the one who is responsible for the Aeronautics Act. I think I indicated in answer to a question asked by the leader of the opposition that the government had decided, under the assignment of duties act, to give to the Minister of Trade and Commerce full responsibility for Trans-Canada Air Lines. There is nothing abnormal about that procedure. There is nothing illogical about that procedure. It does not make for duplication of services as outlined by the leader of the opposition and other speakers. It does not make for irresponsible operation, because there are other operations of government which are in the same category and handled in the same manner. I can think of the C.B.C., which is not responsible to the Minister of Transport but to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann). There is the national film board. It might be responsible to the Minister of Transport or the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). The government has seen fit to make it responsible to another minister.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not want to be interrupted, but I shall answer the hon. member's questions after I have completed my remarks, if I may be allowed. After all this is not a debate in committee; it is a debate on the principle of the bill with the Speaker in the chair.
I say, therefore, that these duties concerning Trans-Canada Air Lines were assigned to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in nc wise differently than in the case of many other bodies under government jurisdiction. I do not see any difference between the operation of T.C.A. being under the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the operation of

Canadian National Railways being under the Minister of Transport. I see no difference between that and the national harbours board, for instance, which is a government agency responsible to a minister; or again the Canadian Commercial Corporation, which to me seems to be along the same lines. I cannot see how that arrangement hampers in any way the efficiency of Trans-Canada Air Lines or of the operation of the Aeronautics Act. I cannot follow the argument because, in one word, if T.C.A. were made responsible to the Minister of Transport there would be no difference in the operation of the air line. The Trans-Canada Air Lines, is a wholly-owned government subsidiary of the Canadian National Railways, if you will, with full powers to operate along certain lines given in its charter. There would be absolutely no difference, if that change were made, from what is now in effect under the present arrangement. Having T.C.A. responsible to another minister does not in any way, I submit to the house, hamper the efficiency of its operations, because it is the government which decides the policy, with regard to both civil aviation generally and the T.C.A., and both the government and T.C.A. make full use of the advice which the air transport board and the civil aviation staff give it in dealing with matters of policy such as these.
I want to complete, if I may at this stage, dealing with the statement made by the leader of the opposition and then to come back to the statements of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. The leader of the opposition made an indirect suggestion or an implied suggestion which was not terribly strong, although it was more ^affirmative than it was the other evening, namely, that the government had not sufficiently fostered the development of civil aviation, that duplication and separation had hampered development of private aviation, and that there were not the number of private services that we should have or that we were entitled to.
I say to him and to the house that that statement is not accurate. I say to him that that statement is far removed from the truth. There is an extensive network of services. I see the leader of the opposition coming in now. I was attempting to reply to the second point he made in his statement, where he intimated by inference -although not terribly strongly at the beginning, more strongly toward the end- that the government had not sufficiently fostered the development of civil aviation, and that duplication and separation had hampered development of private aviation so that there were not the number of private operators
Aeronautics Act
that there should be. Before the hon. gentleman came in I was making the point that that statement was not according to the facts and that that statement was not accurate.

speechtext: According to your estimate; not according to the facts.

speechtext: I see the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) does not like the kind of speech I am making, and therefore I get these interruptions which are hard to follow and even harder to understand.

speechtext: I am not intrigued with it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I am making the statement now that there is an extensive network of services covering every area of Canada, over the most remote regions and areas of our country. Some of these services are scheduled air lines; others are non-scheduled and secondary air lines; and still others are charter services which operate from a fixed base covering the whole surrounding area without any regular route pattern. In fact, I have before me a statement which indicates that there are no less than some 650 licences granted as of this day to the various kinds of air carriers that I mentioned a moment ago, some of them scheduled air carriers, others non-scheduled, others charter air carriers, others flying clubs, and others specialty air carriers.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt the minister, but he is not suggesting, is he, that flying clubs can be regarded as charter service or route services?;

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
No. Flying clubs are not regarded as such services. If I conveyed that impression, I should not have done so. I have a list of the charter services which I could give, but I do not think the house is interested. The development of private operators has proceeded at a far more rapid rate of expansion than the leader of the opposition led us to believe the other evening and again this evening.
Let me make a statement of today's position. There are at the moment some 200 operators. Some of those operators have more than one licence. About half those are small charter operators and the assets of those 100 operators were valued in 1948 at $6,300,000 as compared to 1945 when the value was placed at $434,000. That in itself shows a considerable development in this division of the air transport industry. The development of this group is also reflected in the number of employees, which increased from 128 in 1945 to 648 in 1949. Payrolls for salaries and wages increased in even greater proportion, from $200,000 in 1945 to $1,630,000 in 1949. Total passenger miles increased from 774,000 in 1945 to 7,866,000 in 1949. The

Aeronautics Act
carriage of goods to places otherwise difficult of access is reflected in an increased ton mileage, from 31,000 in 1945 to 754,000 in 1949. Mail services to remote areas also show substantial advances, from less than 2,000 ton miles in 1945 to over 12,000 ton miles in 1949. Total mileage flown in 1949 by 304 aircraft was 12,194,000 as compared with 841,000 in 1945 by only 26 aircraft. That in itself gives some idea of the expansion which took place in the field of civil aviation.
Private operators other than C.P.A. had gross revenues of less than $1 million in 1945 and today they have gross revenues of from $7 million to $8 million, which is a rate of increase far greater than that of T.C.A.
These services are expanding as rapidly as the economic position of the country will allow, and this without subsidy. That is something of which the country ought well to be proud.
The leader of the opposition seems to be of the opinion that this act is expanding or increasing the functions of the board. I put on record a statement indicating that the object of the act was to clarify the responsibilities of the board. In fact, we are not expanding the responsibilities; we are in one instance taking away some of the responsibilities of the air transport board.
The leader of the opposition says that civil aviation is being stifled in Canada, and he referred to what he thought should be done. I disagree strongly with that statement. I think that civil aviation, both within and outside Canada, has developed tremendously; it has developed by leaps and bounds in the post-war period and again within the last year. The leader of the opposition says, "If you look at a map of the air routes of Canada, you will be surprised at the lack of aerial routes in this country."'I have a map before me now. I say just the contrary to what the leader of the opposition has said. Practically every part of this country is covered, in some form or another, by aerial routes today. There are the great Trans-Canada Air Lines operating from one end of the country to the other; air routes going north and south; and not just a few, as suggested by my hon. friend, but many feeder lines going into the northern part of Alberta and Saskatchewan, into northern Manitoba, up into the Northwest Territories, then on the coast of British Columbia and again in Quebec and the maritimes.
This map indicates to me that there has been considerable expansion. If my hon. friend means that the expansion has not been nearly that which he would like to see, and that which we would all like to see, I agree

with him, because as a matter of fact I would like to see private domestic and T.C.A. routes and international routes taken on in far greater numbers. But we must have regard to the economic position of the country. We must not forget that these services are not directly subsidized as they are in the United States. We must not forget either that we cannot have a curtailment of government expenditure, as my hon. friend has been preaching and as he would want the government to practise, and still have these services both in Canada and outside Canada expanded, because it takes a tremendous amount of money, as my hon. friend knows, for the expansion of domestic and international air routes.
Again with reference to the question of expansion, I wish to deal with the two international air agreements which were entered into between Canada and the United States, and Canada and the United Kingdom, by which international aviation was expanded tremendously. Because of our agreement with the United States we received, over and above the routes which we already had, three new routes, a new trans-border route between Montreal and New York; a new route for C.P.A. between Canada and Australasia by way of Honolulu; a new route between Canada and the Bahamas by way of Tampa-St. Petersburg. These are expansions which were due in large part to the survey work done by the air transport board.
Then again our air agreement with the United Kingdom gave us several new routes and traffic stops which we did not possess heretofore. Because of this agreement, which was signed in August of 1949, less than a year ago, Trans-Canada Air Lines on its service to the United Kingdom from Montreal and Gander will be able to carry traffic between the United Kingdom and Ireland, the Azores and Iceland.
Canada, furthermore, because of that agreement, is given full traffic rights at Hong Kong, a new route which is operated by C.P.A. from Vancouver through Alaska, the Aleutians to Japan, China, Hong Kong and beyond. Some few days ago I announced that consideration was being given to an intermediate route because the United States defence forces were contemplating closing down the Aleutian base at Shemya.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Is that still the position? They are closing that base?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not aware as yet of any change in the position from the statement I made the other day.
Then Canada now has full traffic rights at Fiji on its route from Vancouver to Honolulu

and on to Australia. Again Trans-Canada Air Lines' position with reference to the Caribbean has been advanced tremendously, particularly on its route to Bermuda and the British colonies. It has been granted additional rights at Barbados, Antigua and British Guiana. Surely the leader of the opposition could not have had these in mind when he said that aviation is being stifled in this country. I think aviation is advancing-perhaps not as rapidly as we would all wish- but certainly in accordance with our economic position.
If there is to be a greater and a faster expansion the question arises as to who is to pay for it, if it be not the taxpayer of this country in some form or another.
I was making the argument when the leader of the opposition was not here that there seems to be variance among the members of the opposition with reference to aeronautics generally. By that I mean that some of the policies advocated by one member are in contradiction to those advocated by another. The leader of the opposition seemed to state that we were not going far enough or fast enough; whereas the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins) asked a question which indicated that we were going too fast, and that the cost of expansion of T.C.A. services was too great.
I should like to deal more briefly with the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). I am sure he will pardon me if I do not deal too extensively with those remarks. The hon. member repeated some of the arguments made by his leader, particularly those having to do with responsibility of T.C.A. and air services generally to one minister, and I shall not repeat my answer to that. But he criticized ministerial powers over the board. I would like to say to him that the ministerial powers apply to the licensing function of the board, and not to its general economic and administrative regulations with reference to carriers. One thing that must not be forgotten is that even the routes which are assigned to T.C.A. are approved by the government and not by any one minister.
The hon. member stated, as did the leader of the opposition, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) decided the T.C.A. routes. I have to repeat here what I said before. While I am a member of the committee on railways and shipping, I was not present when the statement was made. I would be surprised if it was made in the language that the leader of the opposition suggested it was made; but my information is that the committee records will indicate
Aeronautics Act
that the Minister of Trade and Commerce said the government decided what routes were to be operated by T.C.A.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Don't you remember he said that Polymer was his enterprise?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
We are dealing with T.C.A. now. In fact that is what the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act provides, and it is a fact that the government also decides the international routes.
It was suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra that a portion of the amendment which permits the board to exempt international scheduled carriers from a finding of public convenience and necessity is an undesirable limitation. Well, in fact, it is merely a simplification of the procedure for formal licence of such carriers in the United States. I think in fact the leader of the opposition made the same argument when he said that the air transport board should be an independent body just as the civil aeronautics board is in the United States.
I would have some doubts about that position because we saw what the position of the civil aeronautics board was with reference to an application by T.C.A. which was before it for months before a decision was rendered. I think it would not be an effective procedure to have a finding of public convenience and necessity, when the government decides what the route to be followed is by virtue of an international air agreement. That is the position in Canada. We would like to remove that finding of public convenience and necessity in so far as that aspect is concerned, because we think that procedure would operate more effectively otherwise. There were a number of other suggestions, but I do not think it opportune to go into them at the present time. Perhaps there will be opportunity when we have discussion of the act, section by section, in committee.

Aeronautics Act
It may be thought at first blush that the section under discussion should be removed. It is our great desire in the maritime provinces to see this Chignecto canal become a reality instead of a political talking point such as it has been for the last quarter century.
This item deals with the administration of the canal service. In commenting on this canal service I intend to scratch where it itches most. The canal system of Canada is one of the greatest in the world. For the transportation of free freight there is no canal service in the world to equal it. The large Suez and Panama canals charge commodity tolls ranging from 75 cents to $1.10 per ton, or perhaps more. I should like to indicate the position if our canals charged* similar tolls, although I am not urging that that be done. I have received estimates of the total tonnage of freight moving through our canals yearly and these vary from 25 million tons to 50 million tons. In addition there are no charges for vessels of nations other than

Supply-Transport
Canada. It is all free. If tolls were imposed on freight passing through these canals then at the rates I have quoted it would bring in a revenue to the Dominion of Canada of anywhere from $25 million, to $40 million annually. As I said a moment ago, however, I do not want to persuade the minister to break faith with the people of the provinces for whom the canals were constructed by now taxing them and calling it a toll, freight charge or whatever you wish.
The point I want to make is that so far as canals are concerned they appear in the estimates as a service to the people, and that is the proper way to do it. Every time I see it in the estimates it brings to my mind the contrast that exists so far as the province of Prince Edward Island is concerned. Under an agreement with the federal government we were given the assurance of a connection with the mainland on our entry into union in 1873. The ferry service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland should be listed as a service in the estimates. It should not be called a handout, and it should not be pointed out that there is a deficit on the ferry system from the operation of the boats.
We do not know whether or not there is a deficit. We never receive any statements concerning it, and we know nothing about it. It is true the Minister of Transport may get a statement from the subcontractors who provide the service. Whether he does or does not, the question is one of providing a service for which we paid well in 1873. When we ask for fulfilment of the terms of confederation, as we have often done, when we ask for extra service during the tourist season we are told that they will try it out but if it does not pay they will not provide it in 1951. The terms under which we entered union were that we would have proper communication with the mainland. As I have often said before, all you have to do is read the terms. If there is a deficit forced on us by the subcontractors, the Canadian National Railways, we do not want it to appear as such in the estimates and have it broadcast across Canada that there is a deficit. There is no deficit because it is a service that the dominion government should provide in payment of their debt to us in the same way that we have paid for everything we have got from them under the contract of 1873.
Let the service be listed in the estimates in the same way as canals. Over $8 million is to be voted this year for administration, operation, maintenance, construction and improvements with respect to canals. All these matters are covered by the word "service". On the other hand, when there is a small deficit of a million dollars or so on the 
ferry system between Prince Edward Island and the mainland we are saddled with it, and are told it is a handout and a deficit. It should be treated in the same way as canals. I am not going to go further into the matter. I hope that some day Coueism may have an effect on the minister and that he will see the matter from a bookkeeping standpoint. If he cannot do that, I hope he will look at it from the point of view of the fulfilment of the terms of confederation.

I am glad the hon. member has completed his remarks. I have no objection to his making that speech as often as he likes but I hope he will make it on the proper item. We are dealing with canal service now and not with the Prince Edward Island ferry.

461. Canals-operation and maintenance, $4,398,395.

There is an increase in expenditure of $553,315 this year compared with last year. Some of the more outstanding increases appear in temporary assistance, an increase of nearly $100,000; permanent positions, an increase of about $240,000; and casuals, an increase of $70,000. Will the minister explain that to us? I should also point out that there is an increase in materials and supplies of $99,000. Can the minister point out the reasons for these increases?

The increase of $553,315 is made up as follows: Salaries, materials and supplies, repairs to equipment and structures. Under salaries there are annual increases in certain cases amounting to some

$30,000, $5, $10, or $20 a month. Basic rate increases amount to $212,000. Thirty additional positions-
Why is that?

That is engineering, clerical maintenance-$62,000. Reclassifications and promotions, $11,000; other net increases, $19,000. As !to materials and supplies there is the increased cost of items required in the maintenance of canal properties, uniforms for lockmasters, bridge men and canal men, totalling $99,000. As to repairs to equipment and structures, there is an additional provision for maintenance of canal mobile equipment and various types of structures amounting to $25,000. Then there are other net increases, $19,000 odd.

Why is the amount for travelling expenses under this item so heavy? I notice that last year it was $26,625, and this year it is $27,825, an increase it must toe admitted of $1,000. In view of the size of the item it is not so much, but why do they need that much for travelling expenses?

As the member for Kamloops knows, this item of operation and maintenance of canals covers not only the main canals extending along the route of the St. Lawrence waterway and the great lakes, but also secondary canals. In conjunction with the operation and maintenance of these canals, there is a great amount of travelling to be done. For instance, the cost of the operation of cars has not decreased; on the contrary it has increased. I am informed that explains the increase in that particular item.

I take it there has been no increase in the mileage of canals. We still have only the same mileage to keep up, and it does seem strange that there would toe an increase in the staff. Permanent positions have gone up from 794 to 836, that is an increase of 42. Against that, of course, there are 11 fewer temporary employees. Then, for the casual employees, who I presume are over and above the permanents and temporaries, there is an increase of $73,000. In this year, why should there be an increase in this vote of $500,000, when the total vote last year was under $4 million? It seems to me that is an increase of over 12 per cent. I wonder why it is necessary to have such a large increase? Surely, this work could be done with a smaller vote than the minister is requesting at this time.

With regard to the first question, namely, why should there be such an increase in positions, I am informed by the director of canals that is largely due to

the number of transfers from temporaries to permanents. Then, my hon. friend asked why should there be such an increase in the vote of almost $500,000? He will remember that during the war we did really little or no repairs on the canal systems.
But this is over last year's vote.

Yes, I know, and that is the point I am trying to make. We were not able to do all the repairs in one year that the canals required. I was saying that during the war years no repairs were made at all. We did not have the materials, we did not have the men, and the costs were high. With the normal period back again, we proceeded to do a number of necessary repairs which have to be made from time to time. Those repairs cannot be carried on right through the year, but some can only be made when the water is out of the canals. Other work has to be done at certain times in the year. On the main canals of the great lakes and St. Lawrence waterway, the costs of repairs and maintenance have increased, as have the costs of operation, because of the salary increases which have gone into effect from time to time.

Why should there be that increase this year as compared with .last year? Surely the price of materials has not gone up to that extent within the last twelve months? It looks to me as though this may be a case where the estimate has not been kept down as it might have been. It is a very large increase in the item in a normal year. At least this year should be no different from last year. The war has been over for five years, and the vote last year was $3,800,000, which was sufficient to carry out the repairs and maintenance. Why should we require an additional half million dollars this year?

A moment ago I gave a breakdown of the items which showed the increase of $553,000. I do not think I can explain it much more than that. It is not a detailed statement of the amount, and I do not think my hon. friend would expect me to give him that, but it is a breakdown under the various headings.

But it is not for construction and improvement. They are covered by the next item. This is merely for operation and maintenance-ordinary operation and maintenance. Yet there is an increase in that vote of approximately 12 per cent.

I am informed that the maintenance and improvement of canals and canal services is rather closely interlocked. If

my hon. friend looks at the other vote, which is No. 462, he will see a considerable decrease.
It is under $200,000.
So, having regard to the fact that the two are interlinked, the increase is not abnormal.

Mr. Chairman, surely when we ask a question on one item we should not be tossed over to the other. This is getting into what the New Yorker calls the department of utter confusion. We should be able to say on this item 461 that last year you spent $3,845,000. This year you are estimating for $4,398;000. Now, without getting down to the last dollar, or even the last thousand dollars, surely it must be possible, and I think we should ask for it, to have a definite statement as to the reason for that significant increase. It seems to me unsatisfactory to have it said that we should look at item 462, where we do find a decrease. I think we should deal with each of these items on its merits, and we should have something which, on the face of it, shows the reason for the increase. At the moment we have nothing except what we are so often asked to take, the assurance of the minister, which I have no doubt is given in good faith.
We have had a strong indication that we should tighten up our belts. The Minister of Finance gives it as his considered opinion that we are not doing our job properly, and I doubt if we could have a more expert opinion than his, because he knows better than we do what we should find out and do not. I believe, therefore, we should get much more information than the minister has given us yet.
I am sorry I have no further information to give.

In his first explanation a
moment ago, the minister said one of the main reasons for the increase was the deferred costs of repairs and maintenance, which had been carried over from the war and which he was trying to catch up. It has been pointed out that the increase is some $550,000. If one looks at the details where one might expect to find the expenses of materials and so on, we find that materials have gone up just under $100,000; repairs and upkeep have gone up $5,000; repairs and upkeep of buildings have gone up $22,000, accounting for $127,000 out of $550,000; so it seems to me the minister's explanation that the main cause of the increase is an effort to catch up with repairs and deferred maintenance is hardly borne out by the detail which is given under this estimate itself.

I also point out that in the detail of the item at page 289-and this is apart from the staff itself; the staff is all set out in detail- there are twelve general items or charges for expenditure such as overtime; allowances; travelling expenses; telephones, telegrams and postage; printing, stationery and office equipment; material and supplies; rentals- land and equipment; repairs and upkeep of equipment; repairs and upkeep of buildings and works; express, freight and cartage; light, power and water; and professional and special services. One would have thought that, having gone through that list of twelve headings, each with its amplification and expansion, we would have covered about everything and that there would not be anything left. But we come to the thirteenth item, which is sundries, $31,170, an increase of about $2,300 over last year. After that expanded list of detail, I must confess that I cannot see what you could get in under the hearing of sundries and why you want $31,000 for it. In keeping with the fact that there has been no real explanation of why we should have a general increase of over half a million dollars-I do not think the minister has given us any reason to justify the increase -I think we should move a reduction. Perhaps the minister would like an opportunity to explain what these various things are for.

Yes. The hon. member for Kamloops referred to a statement which I had made, that a large amount was for deferred maintenance. He himself read materials and supplies; and they amount to almost $100,000.
Yes, I said that.

repairs to equipment and structures, which he said amounted to some $9,000 or $10,000. In the breakdown it is $26,000.

The increase on repairs to equipment and structures amounts to $25,960, which is almost $26,000.
Not as given in the estimates. It is $22,000 in the estimates.

It is the breakdown of the increase of $553,315 which he is seeking, and I am trying to give it to him. One of the items of increase is repairs to equipment and structures, which amounts to $25,960. Before I come to that, perhaps I should give my hon. friend the breakdown of the item of sundries, $31,170. This is for miscellaneous expenses on the various canal units. In any event, there are several hundred miles of canals. The breakdown is as follows: Flowers and

seeds $805; unemployment insurance, casual, $1,923; navigation charts, $3,000; icing $25; bonding, $40; garage rent, $220; damage claims, $2,800; advertising, $800; laundry and sanitary services, $1,482; compensation allowance, $500; removal of obstructions, $200; dockage, $375; other unforeseen expenses, $19,000. Then with reference to the general item which members interested seem to have some qualms about, the increase of $553,000 is due in large part, as I stated, to the work that we have had to do. The increase in labour rates alone amounts to at least $250,000 of that $553,000.

Now we are
coming to it.
We have had to pay a certain amount of overtime.
Why?

Because of reclassifications by the Department of Labour in working conditions in the various canals from time to time. The canal system is unionized and the organizations make representations to us for new working agreements. I should not say to us; they make representations to the Department of Labour. Any representations to us are referred to the Department of Labour and the Department of Labour fixes the rates. Very often we have to reclassify labourers, riggers, canal operators, canal men and lockmasters. More than half of this is due to increased rates.

I observe, for instance, at page 287, that there are quite a few instances of increases in staff. I notice, about halfway down the page, several new technicians. Does that arise through different labour conditions?-because we understand that we are dealing with exactly the same physical extent of canal system.

I think I gave to the hon. member for Kamloops a breakdown of the technical positions. No, the technical position would not arise from a reclassification of operating labour. The technical positions, I take it, are civil servants, and if there is an increase-I do not know which one my hon. friend has in view-it would result from a reclassification by the civil service commission. There have been a considerable number of reclassifications all along the line in the various departments, particularly in the large departments like public works, transport, trade and commerce and mines and resources, which is now divided into two new departments. But the question the hon. member for Greenwood addresses to me does not relate to the answer I have given to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra.
Supply-Transport

I notice that there has been an increase in canal men, grade II, from 104 to 123; and in canal men, grade I, from 68 to 82. As to the higher grades, there is no change. Why is it necessary to take on all these extra men?
No extra men-
That is one question I should like answered. Another is this. The cost of having casual help is going up from $120,000 to $193,000. Why is there that increase in the casual help?

With reference to the canal men-and I did not catch the second question -the increase in canal men from 104 to 123, and the question as to why it is necessary to have the additional number of men, may I say that there are no additional canal men engaged. The 21 are temporaries who have become permanent. With reference to the casual help, more casual helpers or seasonal men have been taken on to do some of this deferred maintenance that I referred to a moment ago on the main line canals.

Marine service-
465. Marine service administration, $18,970.

Under this group of headings, I should like to ask the minister a general question as to the way in which the organization of the marine service is set up. I understand there is a director of marine services, a marine superintendent, a supervisor of nautical services, a chief of aids to navigation. Then there is what is called pilotage administration which I assume is another officer. I should like to find how all these administrative officials relate to each other. For example, do they all report to the director of marine services, and how does that work out, because there is a great multiplicity of them? I should like to know exactly how the organization stands.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, this vote covers marine services administration. This appropriation is a small one and provides for the salaries and other expenses of the office of the director of marine services. The office supervises the following branches of marine services: aids to navigation. Aids to navigation is a branch in itself, as we shall see later on. This vote does not provide for the expenditures of that branch, but for the direction of it under the supervision of the director of marine services.
Nautical services is another division which is responsible to the director, and later on

Supply-Transport
we shall have a vote covering that branch. Marine agencies is also a fairly substantial vote.
Is that vote 470?
Yes.

Will the
minister explain that a little; it does not explain itself.

Yes. There are some 10 marine agencies across Canada. I will take Ontario first. There is one in Prescott, and there is one in Parry Sound. On the west coast there is one at Victoria and one at Prince Rupert. On the east coast there is one at Saint John, New Brunswick, and one at St. John's, Newfoundland; there is one at Halifax, there is one at Charlottetown, one at Montreal and one at Quebec. The responsibilities of the agents are to look after the maintenance of aids to navigation, and they have some responsibility for steamers, too.
Then I go on and explain the operation of the marine floating equipment.

May I ask
the minister a question about these agencies first? I think he said that the chiefs of those marine services were responsible for certain things. Did he mean by that the agencies?
Yes.
Is the agency what it sounds like, an independent man who is at arm's length from the department, and not an ordinary civil servant?

Oh, yes; he is responsible for the marine agency in his branch. Again I take Prescott. We have a marine agent who is responsible for an area in the St. Lawrence river extending from Sarnia on the west to the Quebec border on the east.
The word "agency" does not suggest that he is at arm's length from anybody. He is an employee.
Oh, no.

item 465. The minister has answered certain questions which I asked with regard to the whole marine service administration. I have another question. What about purchasing done for all these various bodies? How is that done?

that I suggest it might be relevant to ask it in connection with the whole question of administration. However, if the minister prefers to answer later, that is all right.

Marine service-
467. Nautical service administration, $194,262.

This item has to do with nautical services administration. When we turn to the details on page 290 we find that $300,000 of the reduction shown of $296,408, in fact more than the total reduction, is being taken off the vocational training for merchant seamen. The allowance is being cut from $350,000 to $50,000, and it is rather ironical to read the next two items in the details. They are, "campaign stars, $4,000; war medals, $6,000." The reduction means that there is going to be very little vocational training available for these merchant navy veterans during the present fiscal year. I would ask the minister to explain the present position with regard to this vocational training. I find in the annual report of the department for the year ended March 31, 1949, that this particular activity under the nautical service branch is described as follows:
In association with the Department of Veterans Affairs, rehabilitation and vocational training of qualified merchant seamen who served at sea during the second world war.
And further down we find the last job of this branch is:
Issue of medals to merchant seamen in recognition of service at sea during the second world war.
I am not going to repeat at length the stand I have taken for years with regard to these merchant navy veterans. But the picture is that only a very limited number of them are able to get vocational training, and none of them are able to get any educational benefits. In addition they get no war veterans allowance, civil service preference, hospitalization, or the various other benefits available for the men in the other arms of the service. I had hoped that while there was some extension of the regulations last year, during the present fiscal year much better provision would be made for those men who served in the merchant navy. I wish the minister would explain to the committee whether there is to be any further consideration given to these men and at the same time explain why the benefits are limited to those who had a manning-pool contract. We find at page 54 of the annual report of the department the statement of those who were eligible.

I have had young men come into my office in Vancouver who were too young to sign a manning-pool contract. They were not asked to sign a contract by the officials. I have had other young men come in who were put on a Canadian vessel without ever being asked to sign a contract. One man was transferred in Egypt. He had been in hospital there, had been on a British ship and was sent out on a Canadian ship, and nothing was said to him about signing any contract. As a result of not having a contract he is not eligible for any of those benefits. I think these restrictions are much too drastic. There should be a broadening of the qualifications so that more of these men could become eligible for the benefits.
Occasionally we encounter the reply that these men of the merchant navy did not want to serve, that they tried to escape war service and therefore joined the merchant navy. There is one effective answer to that, and it is that the casualties in the merchant navy were higher in proportion to those serving in that force than they were in. any of the three other forces. It will be recalled that during the war a board dealt with young men who were called up. I had the opportunity recently to speak to one of our most responsible citizens who had served on a mobilization board in Vancouver; he told me that time and again young men came in who had been found unfit to join the other forces, and for that reason had been turned down, yet while they could have had exemption insisted upon joining the merchant navy because of their determination to do their bit.
It does not sit well now for anyone to say that men who served in the merchant navy were not willing to play their part. That certainly was not so on the Pacific coast, and I do not think it was so on the Atlantic or in the St. Lawrence. I have never been able to see why the Department of Transport has not taken the position that these men were the fourth arm of the service, and that they should be given every chance to be re-established.
This year the situation has been made much worse because of the fact that so many Canadian vessels-I believe the minister gave the number as ninety-three-have been transferred to British registry. In most cases the crews of those ships were discharged; they could not live on the British rates of pay. I think the minister will admit that most of them have lost their jobs as sailors and are now "on the beach."
Apparently there is no provision whatever to give these men vocational training. I believe they should be helped to re-establish themselves in some other fields. I shall not
Supp ly-Transport
take further time of the committee, but I would ask the minister to explain the position, with the hope that it will be possible for him to recommend to the government a change in the provisions made for these men.

I, too, have been hoping that the minister and his colleague, the Minister of Veterans Affairs, would have been able to do more along the lines of vocational training than has been done in the past. However, it appears now from the reduction in the vote for vocational training that, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has said, that work is just about wiped out.

May I interrupt the hon. member? I did not wish to say this when the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra was speaking. I must point out however that there is no reduction in the vote. When the main estimates were prepared the policy had not been announced of extending vocational training. So that the hon. member may drop that from his remarks. I shall deal with this at greater length at another time. There is no intention however of not carrying out the statement made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs and by myself toward the end of the last session.
I am very glad to hear that, and I have no wish to labour the matter further. Would the minister tell the committee now what is being done in this connection?

The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra closed his remarks by saying, having in mind the statement I made the other day on the merchant shipbuilding and operations program to the effect that a large number of ships-ninety-three I believe- had been transferred to British registry, that many men would be out of work. I also stated at that time that there were some nine thousand seamen employed, although the report of the maritime commission had suggested seven thousand, in accordance with its over-all program.
Then the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra states that no provision was made to look after these merchant seamen. The policy announced toward the end of the last session by myself, in conjunction with the Minister of Veterans Affairs, was to take care of that. In other words, the Prime Minister made it clear that one of the reasons for the policy of extending the vocational training to merchant seamen was to assist those who would be laid off. These estimates were prepared before that statement was made, because they have to be made up some time in advance.

Supply-Transport
Then I am sure hon. members would like to know how much has been paid thus far. The total amount reimbursed to the Department of Veterans Affairs up to February 28, 1950, for 225 applicants was $112,000. There would be in the supplementary estimates a substantial amount'-I do not know just how much, but perhaps in the neighbourhood of $150,000. So that we intend to carry out the policy which was announced.
The hon. member says no further consideration has been given. Well, no further consideration has been given since the announcement was made to extend the benefits to merchant seamen. I do not think I can add much more at this time.
What are the qualifications required by a seaman to receive vocational training?
I put that information on record last year. I would state roughly that a merchant seaman must have been in receipt of one of the two bonuses.
What is the age limit?

Vocational training for the rehabilitation of merchant seamen under the order which was announced applied to those seamen under thirty years of age who were in receipt of either the war service bonus or a special bonus.

With the great decrease in the Canadian merchant service it follows that a great many merchant seamen will be thrown out of employment. Because of the nature of a sailor's employment I imagine it would be more difficult for him to fit into other kinds of work than it would be for the ordinary landsman. I am not going to criticize the minister for what has happened to our merchant service, because I do not know enough about it to criticize intelligently. It may be that no responsibility falls upon the minister. It may be that because of world conditions over which this government has no control it was found the Canadian merchant service could not be self-supporting.
I believe we are moving into a new position in matters of this kind. Where employment fails through.no fault of the government, through no fault of the employer and certainly through no fault of the employees engaged in the service, there is a responsibility upon the government to fit these men for some other work. We may find it difficult to accept that, but we are moving into new times where the welfare of the individual worker is becoming of increasing importance to the whole question-I put it this way for lack of better words-of peace and war. It has become a part of our state policy of which we must take cognizance.

Let us not forget that for the past four or five years the United States government has been providing huge sums of money to sustain populations in other parts of the world. That is not done just because the United States government is kind-hearted, it is done because the welfare of workers in any part of the world is important for the peace of the world today. If it is important for one nation to take action because of conditions in another nation, surely it is much more important inside a country itself. In fitting these men for employment I think we will have to go beyond the narrow conditions that applied after the war.
I have no worked-out plan, but I submit the government should take the matter under advisement. It is not a good thing for this country to have men who are anxious to work looking for work and not finding it in their chosen employment.
I do not think the government can explain their way out of the transfer of ninety-three of our ships to British registry.
A discussion of that will be entirely out of order. There will be a time and place for that discussion.
The minister answered the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and in fact he raised the matter himself, and then there was the statement made just now by the hon. member for Vancouver East.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Cape Breton South will realize that if this matter was mentioned in the speeches of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the hon. member for Vancouver East it was in connection with unemployment which that situation had created and also in connection with vocational training.

That is exactly what I am going to talk about. Seamen are unemployed because ships have been transferred to British registry. I am not quarrelling with the suggestion to retrain seamen in co-operation with veterans affairs, but I do quarrel with the reason why that should be done. This unemployment problem has been created by transferring ships to British registry.
This is not something new; this is just history repeating itself because we did exactly the same thing after the first war. We built up an effective merchant marine staffed with British officers but when the war was over those British officers were demobilized and the sailors were beached. Most of the ships were sold to Japan and other countries in the Far East. In the present case I have taken the same position as that taken by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. We have worked on this problem in committee

and in the house. We have always taken the position that regulations and legislation applicable to members of the armed services should be made applicable to merchant seamen. They worked on ships that were armed and did what was perhaps one of the most effective jobs in the war.
Basic to this question of training seamen who are unemployed is the fact that ships have been transferred to British registry while others have been sold. I do not think that can be justified?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I must ask the hon. member to confine his remarks to the item under discussion.
I am confining my remarks to the item. I am simply following up the discussion which was permitted and which was raised by the minister in his answer to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra.

On a point of order, I cannot allow the hon. member to put in my mouth words which were not spoken. I did not raise the subject; it was raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. However, the hon. member was speaking on the item and in the course of his remarks he referred to the ninety-three ships. If the hon. member wants to enter into a discussion of the policy adopted by the government, I can deal with the matter now but I do not think this is the time to do it. If the hon. member wants to speak until eleven o'clock all right, but there are one or two things I would have liked to say to the hon. member since there is perhaps some information he is not aware of concerning his statements.

I have not made any statement as yet; I was simply beginning to make a statement which the minister apparently is afraid to let me complete. If the minister wants me to drop this subject so that he can take up something else, I am quite prepared to do so and bring it up later on in his estimates. I am sure I can show him that I know a lot more about this subject than he thinks I do. If he is sparring for time, all right. The minister is a very obliging fellow and I certainly would like to accommodate him. If he will ask me now to drop the subject and take it up later, I am quite willing to do that, but I am not admitting that I am out of order because this discussion has been permitted.

I am asking the hon. member to be good enough to postpone his discussion because he is out of order. When we reach item 525 concerning the maritime commission I shall be glad to deal with his statement. The hon. member will then have full opportunity to go into the subject which he wants to deal with under an item which does not concern it at all.
Supply-Transport
The minister has asked me to drop this because I am out of order. I will not drop it because I am not out of order.
The chairman decides that, not the hon. member.
It has been decided already by your raising the matter in answering the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. You should have been called out of order and we would not be wrangling about it.

Perhaps I am the one
responsible for getting this discussion off on the wrong foot. I am quite willing to take the blame for that and perhaps the minister should have raised the point of order when I was speaking. In view of the fact he wants to make a statement tonight I will apologize for being out of order so that he can do so, and we will take up the other matter under the report of the maritime commission.

That is not a point of order. That is a demonstration of impudence. He is attempting to tell the chairman how to run the committee. If the minister wants to make a statement I am quite prepared to give him the floor to do so and postpone this discussion, but not because I am out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I want to make it quite clear that there is no doubt in the chairman's mind that the hon. member is entirely out of order when he seeks to discuss the policy of the government in selling certain ships of Canadian registry thereby creating unemployment, and I so rule. When the hon. member mentions that situation in relation to the item under discussion, item 467, nautical service administration, I should like to point out that at page 290 there is a subtitle, "vocational training". If the hon. member wants to argue that vocational training would not have been necessary if that policy had not been followed, that is all right; but it is only complementary to the discussion of the item of vocational training. If he wants to argue with the minister whether or not the government was justified in following the policy it did, then he is entirely out of order. Of course it is quite difficult to settle these matters when some hon. members who are experienced stay on what I might call the borderline. They talk about a certain subject that is extraneous to the discussion and then mention vocational training every now and then. Every few seconds they turn to something else and then come back to vocational training. It is very difficult for the chairman to decide, and I ask the co-operation of the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I know he will relate his remarks to the item under discussion.

Supply-Transport

I am quite prepared to bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, although I do not agree with the reasoning. If we had not sold the ships we would not have had unemployment and it would not have been necessary to have vocational training. We will continue this disoussion later on under the proper item but I am still not admitting I am out of order.

I think it would be most helpful if the minister could tell us what reduction there has been in the last year in the number of men in the Canadian merchant navy. We will then know how many there are who could be helped by vocational training. Of course in addition to that number there will be a further reduction as the policy is continued because the minister has said that the plan is to cut them down to 7,000 or 7,500. Which was it?
In the statement I made I said there were 9,000 employed.
And that the commission recommended that be cut down to 7,000 or 7,500.
I do not think they recommended a cut but in the over-all policy they thought that the number who should always be employed or provided for should be in the neighbourhood of 7,000.
So there will be quite a few hundred more out of employment as that policy is pursued.
I hope not.
Can the minister tell us how many merchant navy men lost their employment in the last year?

I could not tell the hon. member that under this item. I would not have that information. I shall have the information when there is a general discussion under the maritime commission item. I can tell the hon. member one thing, and it deals with the problem raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East who was complaining bitterly about the large number of seamen out of work. There have been only 239 applications following the statement made by myself and the Minister of Veterans Affairs toward the end of the last session.
That may be-

Wait. That gives some indication of those who are affected, and heaven knows we have advertised enough in every possible way. When the number who have applied for vocational training is 239, that shows the house if there are tremendous unemployment problems being created by the transfers.

It may also be an indication that the regulations are much too severe. The minister will remember that no men over thirty can apply for that training. It is also restricted to those men who signed manning pool contracts. Personally I think a great many men have not applied because they know they cannot qualify, and it is about that point I am complaining. We think the regulations should be made easier. This is a very important problem in the coastal cities, and I suggest to the minister that he let the item stand.
Why should the item stand?
You cannot get it through by eleven o'clock.
Certainly it should not stand because of what my hon. friend has said. If there is going to be more discussion on the item then the committee is entitled to that discussion.
There are other points I should like to bring up in connection with the item, and I suggest to the minister that he let it stand.

It is one minute to eleven. Shall it carry?
Item stands.
Progress reported.
